questions.prompt: What are the three core components of the MVC design pattern?

options.text: Model, View, and Controller.
options.explanation: MVC stands for Model, View, and Controller.

options.text: Module, Variable, and Class.
options.explanation: Module, Variable, and Class are general language concepts, not MVC.

options.text: Memory, Vector, and Compiler.
options.explanation: Memory, Vector, and Compiler are computer science terms, not MVC.

options.text: Method, View, and Container.
options.explanation: MVC uses Model and Controller, not Method and Container.

questions.prompt: What is the primary responsibility of the Model layer in MVC?

options.text: To render user interface layouts and respond to gestures.
options.explanation: Rendering UI is the role of the View layer.

options.text: To encapsulate data, storage, and core business rules.
options.explanation: The Model manages application data and domain business rules.

options.text: To coordinate navigation between different iOS view screens.
options.explanation: Navigation coordination belongs to the Controller or Coordinator.

options.text: To capture touch events directly from the hardware screen.
options.explanation: Touch event handling begins in UIKit Views and the window.

questions.prompt: How do the Model and View layers interact in Apple Cocoa MVC?

options.text: The View observes the Model directly through two-way binding.
options.explanation: In Cocoa MVC, the View and Model do not communicate directly.

options.text: The Model retains a strong reference to the root view.
options.explanation: The Model must remain completely decoupled from views.

options.text: They do not interact directly; the Controller mediates all data flow.
options.explanation: Cocoa MVC strictly uses the Controller as an explicit mediator.

options.text: They share global static memory to avoid creating references.
options.explanation: Sharing global memory violates separation of concerns.

questions.prompt: What is the Massive View Controller problem in iOS development?

options.text: When a view controller class consumes more than ten megabytes of RAM.
options.explanation: The problem relates to excessive code responsibilities, not byte size.

options.text: When an app contains more than one hundred view controller classes.
options.explanation: Having many focused view controllers is actually a recommended practice.

options.text: When an iPad screen displays three split view controllers at once.
options.explanation: Split views are a standard iPad layout pattern, not an architecture bug.

options.text: When view controllers become bloated by absorbing networking and layout.
options.explanation: Massive View Controller happens when too many roles crowd one file.

questions.prompt: Why is it difficult to unit test business logic written inside UIViewController?

options.text: Because the code depends on UIKit and the view controller lifecycle.
options.explanation: Testing requires instantiating views and waiting for lifecycle events.

options.text: Because Xcode forbids test targets from importing the UIKit framework.
options.explanation: Test targets can import UIKit without issue.

options.text: Because view controllers cannot be initialized without a physical iPhone.
options.explanation: View controllers can be initialized in simulators or headless tests.

options.text: Because UIViewController methods cannot accept or return integers.
options.explanation: UIViewController methods support standard Swift data types.

questions.prompt: How can table view data source logic be extracted out of a bloated view controller?

options.text: By moving the table view into the app delegate class.
options.explanation: The app delegate handles application-level events, not table views.

options.text: By using a dedicated data source object or Diffable Data Source.
options.explanation: Diffable data sources or custom data source objects remove table logic.

options.text: By replacing the table view with fifty individual labels in code.
options.explanation: Manual labels do not provide reusable scrolling list behavior.

options.text: By declaring all table cell identifiers as global static variables.
options.explanation: Global identifiers do not decouple data source logic from the controller.

questions.prompt: What UIKit feature allows splitting a complex screen into smaller modular controllers?

options.text: NotificationCenter broadcast channels for publishing events.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter is an event bus, not a view controller container.

options.text: Core Data persistent container contexts for local storage.
options.explanation: Core Data is a persistence framework, not a UI modularization tool.

options.text: Child view controllers using addChild and didMove(toParent:).
options.explanation: Child view controllers break large screens into isolated, modular units.

options.text: DispatchQueue concurrent worker queues for background tasks.
options.explanation: GCD worker queues manage concurrency, not UI structure.

questions.prompt: Why should network calls not be placed directly in viewDidLoad?

options.text: Because iOS suspends all network sockets when viewDidLoad runs.
options.explanation: Network sockets function normally during viewDidLoad.

options.text: Because viewDidLoad runs exclusively on private background threads.
options.explanation: viewDidLoad always executes on the main thread.

options.text: Because URLSession cannot be instantiated inside UIViewController classes.
options.explanation: URLSession can be instantiated anywhere in Swift.

options.text: Because it couples the controller to networking and prevents mock testing.
options.explanation: Direct networking in controllers prevents injecting mock responses in tests.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between original 1979 Smalltalk MVC and Apple Cocoa MVC?

options.text: In Smalltalk, Views observed Models directly; in Cocoa, Controllers mediate.
options.explanation: Cocoa MVC routes all communication through the Controller mediator.

options.text: In Smalltalk, Controllers did not exist; they were added by Apple.
options.explanation: Controllers were a fundamental part of original Smalltalk MVC.

options.text: In Smalltalk, Models handled user touch input on mobile screens.
options.explanation: Smalltalk MVC was developed for desktop GUI workstations.

options.text: In Smalltalk, Views compiled directly into machine assembly code.
options.explanation: Smalltalk executed in a bytecode virtual machine environment.

questions.prompt: Where should currency formatting and date formatting logic live in a clean architecture?

options.text: Inside the storyboard XML definition files.
options.explanation: Storyboards define UI hierarchies and layout, not code logic.

options.text: Inside dedicated formatter helpers or model extensions.
options.explanation: Extracting formatting into helpers keeps controllers clean and testable.

options.text: Inside the AppDelegate applicationDidFinishLaunching method.
options.explanation: AppDelegate should not contain screen-specific formatting logic.

options.text: Inside UIKit system drawing methods like drawRect.
options.explanation: drawRect handles direct Core Graphics drawing, not text formatting.

questions.prompt: What risk arises when passing an entire database model directly into a custom view?

options.text: The app immediately crashes with an invalid memory access error.
options.explanation: Passing models into views compiles and runs without memory crashes.

options.text: The custom view is automatically converted into a table view cell.
options.explanation: Views retain their subclass identity regardless of passed parameters.

options.text: The view becomes coupled to that model and cannot be reused elsewhere.
options.explanation: Views should accept simple primitives or view-specific presentation data.

options.text: The Swift compiler generates twenty warnings on every build.
options.explanation: The compiler does not warn about model-view coupling.

questions.prompt: Is MVC completely obsolete and forbidden in modern iOS development?

options.text: Yes, Apple removed UIViewController from the iOS SDK entirely.
options.explanation: UIViewController remains a core component of UIKit.

options.text: Yes, App Store review rejects any app using the MVC pattern.
options.explanation: Apple does not review or reject apps based on internal architecture.

options.text: Yes, the Swift compiler warns when creating a UIViewController.
options.explanation: UIViewController is standard UIKit API with no compiler warnings.

options.text: No, disciplined MVC remains effective for simple screens and apps.
options.explanation: MVC is simple and effective when responsibilities are separated.

questions.prompt: How does separating a network service out of the controller help with automated testing?

options.text: Tests can inject a mock service to return instant fake responses.
options.explanation: Mock services allow deterministic, fast unit tests without live networks.

options.text: Tests bypass the Swift type checker and execute twice as fast.
options.explanation: The Swift compiler always enforces type checking on test code.

options.text: Tests execute on the GPU instead of running on the CPU.
options.explanation: Unit tests run on the CPU within the host process.

options.text: Tests disable memory management to improve simulator boot speed.
options.explanation: Memory management remains active during all automated testing.

questions.prompt: Which component should handle user input validation, such as checking password length?

options.text: The custom UIView subclass that renders the text field.
options.explanation: Views should remain presentational and not make validation decisions.

options.text: The Model layer or a dedicated validation helper object.
options.explanation: Business rules and input validation belong in the Model or dedicated helpers.

options.text: The device operating system kernel graphics pipeline.
options.explanation: The graphics pipeline only handles pixel rasterization.

options.text: The launch storyboard file before the app finishes booting.
options.explanation: Storyboards cannot perform dynamic runtime user input validation.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI address the traditional Massive View Controller problem?

options.text: By requiring all state variables to be stored in an SQL database.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses property wrappers in memory, not SQL tables.

options.text: By compiling every view controller directly into Objective-C classes.
options.explanation: SwiftUI is pure Swift and does not use view controller classes.

options.text: By using declarative views driven by state rather than imperative controllers.
options.explanation: Declarative state-driven views eliminate imperative view controllers.

options.text: By forcing all network requests to run synchronously on the main thread.
options.explanation: SwiftUI encourages asynchronous networking using async/await.

questions.prompt: What is the Massive View Controller problem in iOS, and what causes it?

rubric.criterion: Defines Massive View Controller as a common antipattern where view controllers become bloated with thousands of lines of code.
Identifies causes: tight coupling between UIViewController and view lifecycle, absorbing networking, layout, data sources, and business logic.

questions.modelAnswer:
The Massive View Controller problem is a common iOS antipattern where UIViewController files grow to thousands of lines of code.

It is caused by the tight coupling between UIViewController and the view lifecycle. Because UIViewController owns the view and manages lifecycle events like viewDidLoad, developers often dump all application tasks into it. These tasks include URLSession networking, table view data sources and delegates, constraint layout, navigation routing, and input validation. This violates the Single Responsibility Principle and makes testing difficult.

questions.prompt: Describe three practical techniques to slim down an oversized UIViewController in UIKit.

rubric.criterion: Mentions extracting networking and persistence into dedicated service classes or protocols.
Mentions using child view controllers or custom view subclasses to isolate UI components.
Mentions extracting data sources (such as Diffable Data Source) or formatting and validation helpers into pure Swift types.

questions.modelAnswer:
Here are three practical techniques to slim down an oversized UIViewController:

1. Extract a Network Service: Move all URLSession network requests and JSON decoding into dedicated service classes behind protocols. The controller simply calls the service and receives models.
2. Use Child View Controllers: Break complex screens into modular child view controllers using addChild and didMove(toParent:). Each child manages its own small section of the interface.
3. Extract Data Sources and Formatters: Move table view data source logic into separate data source objects or use UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource. Extract date and currency formatting into pure helper structs.

questions.prompt: Why does keeping business logic out of UIViewController improve unit testing?

rubric.criterion: Explains that testing UIViewController requires loading UIKit views and lifecycle states, which is slow and fragile.
Explains that pure Swift models and helper types can be tested in isolation in milliseconds without UIKit dependencies.

questions.modelAnswer:
Keeping business logic out of UIViewController greatly improves unit testing in two main ways:

First, testing a UIViewController requires initializing UIKit objects, loading view hierarchies, and simulating lifecycle calls like viewDidLoad. This setup is fragile, slow, and prone to UIKit side effects.

Second, extracting business logic into pure Swift structs or classes allows headless unit testing. These pure models have no dependencies on UIKit. Tests can execute in milliseconds, pass in test parameters, and verify calculations deterministically without mocking screen rendering.

questions.prompt: Explain the architectural difference between Smalltalk MVC and Apple Cocoa MVC.

rubric.criterion: Explains that in Smalltalk MVC, the View observes the Model directly via notifications or observers.
Explains that in Apple Cocoa MVC, the Controller acts as an explicit mediator, and Model and View never interact directly.

questions.modelAnswer:
The primary difference between Smalltalk MVC and Apple Cocoa MVC is how the View and Model interact.

In the original Smalltalk MVC architecture from 1979, the View observed the Model directly. When data in the Model changed, the View received notification events and updated itself. The Controller was primarily responsible for capturing user input and sending commands to the Model.

In Apple Cocoa MVC, the View and Model never talk directly. The Controller acts as an explicit mediator. It receives events from the View, updates the Model, and takes data from the Model to configure the View. This makes views more reusable across different data models.

questions.prompt: How does the Coordinator pattern help solve navigation bloat inside view controllers?

rubric.criterion: Explains that view controllers often hardcode transitions using navigationController.pushViewController or segues, creating tight coupling.
Explains that a Coordinator handles navigation and screen flow, allowing view controllers to remain independent of screen routing.

questions.modelAnswer:
In standard UIKit MVC, view controllers often handle their own navigation. They instantiate the next view controller and call navigationController?.pushViewController or present. This creates tight coupling because the current controller must know about future screens and their dependencies.

The Coordinator pattern extracts navigation out of view controllers entirely. A dedicated Coordinator object controls app flow, instantiates view controllers, injects dependencies, and handles screen transitions. When a user taps a button, the view controller delegates the event to its coordinator. This keeps view controllers reusable and isolated from app routing details.
